lesson.title: What Comes Back: Using Return Values
lesson.summary: The value a function returns is not automatically displayed, it must be printed, stored, or used directly in another expression, and that habit is what lets small functions combine into larger programs.
lesson.body:
A function call is an expression, and like every expression in Python, it evaluates to a value: specifically, whatever the function's return statement produced. This value does not announce itself. Running square(5) as a standalone line inside a script produces no visible output at all, even though the function computes 25 internally and hands it back, because evaluating an expression and displaying it are two separate things in Python; only interactive sessions echo bare expressions automatically. To see the result in an ordinary script, you must either print it explicitly, with print(square(5)), or capture it in a variable, with result = square(5), so that it can be used later.

Once a return value is captured or used directly, it behaves exactly like any other value of its type: it can be stored, compared, printed, passed to another function, or combined with other values using operators. If def square(n): return n * n is defined, then total = square(3) + square(4) first calls square(3), getting 9, then calls square(4), getting 16, and finally adds them together, so total ends up as 25. Nothing here is special-cased for function calls; Python evaluates square(3) and square(4) to produce ordinary numbers first, and only then applies the + operator to those numbers, the same way it would if you had written 9 + 16 directly.

This composability is exactly what makes chains of small functions powerful. Suppose you have def celsius_to_fahrenheit(c): return c * 9 / 5 + 32 and def describe_temp(f): return "hot" if f > 85 else "mild" if f > 65 else "cold". You can feed the return value of one directly into the other: describe_temp(celsius_to_fahrenheit(30)). Tracing this, celsius_to_fahrenheit(30) runs first, computing 30 * 9 / 5 + 32, which is 54.0 + 32, which is 86.0, and that 86.0 becomes the argument passed into describe_temp. Inside describe_temp, f is 86.0, so f > 85 is True, and the function returns "hot". The whole nested expression describe_temp(celsius_to_fahrenheit(30)) evaluates to "hot", built entirely from two small, independently testable functions rather than one long block of mixed-purpose code.

A common source of confusion is forgetting that a return value has to go somewhere to be useful. Writing celsius_to_fahrenheit(30) alone on a line, with no print and no assignment, computes 86.0 and then throws that value away, since nothing in the program kept a reference to it. This is easy to miss because the function runs successfully and no error appears; the mistake is silent. Getting into the habit of asking, for every function call you write, "what happens to the value this returns," is what separates code that merely runs from code that actually accomplishes something, exactly the discipline that makes larger programs, built from many small return-producing functions wired together, work correctly.
